background.definition: Giant cell arteritis (GCA), also known as temporal arteritis (TA) when affecting the temporal artery, is a systemic vasculitis involving large and medium-sized arteries. It involves mainly the cranial arteries and in particular the superficial temporal artery. Occurring largely in individuals over the age of 50 years, it can result in infarction and ischemia of distant structures and blindness.

list.listitem: 0.17 new cases annually per 1000 persons over 50 years of Northern European descent.
A systematic review idnetified a pooled incidence rate of giant cell arteritis of 10/100,000 people over 50 years old, and was highest in Scandinavia (22/100,000/year).
Incidence increases with age and peaks in patients >70 years.
More common in women than men, whites than non-whites.
2 per 1000 persons.
A systematic review found a pooled prevalence of 52/100,000 people over age 50 years, with mortality of 20/1000 affected persons.
Possible genetic component (increased incidence in individuals with HLA-DR4).
Possible triggering role of infection (mycoplasma pneumoniae, parvovirus B19 and chlamydia pneumoniae are suspected).
About half of people with GCA or TA also have polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR), and 10% with polymyalgia rheumatica also have TA.
Inflammatory process which is focal and segmental resulting in a maladaptive response to arterial injury.
Cellular immune response involving macrophages, T cells, antigen-presenting cells, macrophage-derived inflammatory cytokines, and HLA molecules.
These changes result in inflammatory changes to the tunica media vasorum and tunica adventitia of arteries; classically involving the arteries of the internal and external carotid arteries.
Occlusion of these vessels results in the clinical findings of headache, jaw claudication, visual changes (blindness) and scalp tenderness.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Smoking (this is true only for women)

list.listitem: Three or more of the five ACR criteria are very useful in making diagnosis. B
Normal ESR is helpful in ruling-out GCA or TA. B
Patients older than 50 with jaw claudication or diplopia and temporal artery beading, prominence, or tenderness should have a temporal artery biopsy. B

British guidelines suggest that for patients with a high clinical probability of GCA (> 50%) and abnormal ultrasound, biopsy may not be necessary. Similarly, low risk patients (< 20%) with normal ultrasound can also avoid biopsy with close clinical follow-up.B

list.listitem:
International Headache Society definition of GCA requires two of the following in a new headache:
Headache developed at the same time as other symptoms or clinical or biological signs of GCA One or both of a) headache has significantly worsened in parallel with worsening of GCA or b) headache has significantly improved or reesolved within 3 days of high dose steroids Headache is associated with scalp tenderness and/or jaw claudication.

Three or more of the following five criteria are 93% sensitive and 91% specific for TA: Age of onset of disease ≥50 years New headache Temporal artery abnormality ESR ≥50 mm/hour Abnormal findings on biopsy of temporal artery
GCA or TA are rare before the age of 50 years.

Limb claudication and differential blood pressure between limbs may occur with involvement of arteries other than the temporal artery. Jaw claudication (LR+ 4.8) and history of polymyalgia rheumatica (LR+ 2.2) also both increase the likelihood of GCA.
The most helpful physical exam findings are temporal artery thickening (LR+ 4.9), temporal artery loss of pulse (LR+ 3.2) and temporal tenderness (LR+ 3.2).

Ophthalmic complications can include anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, central retinal artery occlusion, branch retinal artery occlusion, posterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or choroidal infarction.

A systematic review of 68 studies with 14,037 patients found that jaw claudication, temporal tenderness, temporal artery loss of pulse, and temporal artery thickening were the best predictors of GCA when it was clinically suspected.
Include a detailed opthalmologic and joint examination.
Ask about comorbid conditions such as chronic infection, osteoporosis, hypertension, or diabetes that might predispose the patient to adverse effects of corticosteroids.
Atypical signs and symptoms are seen in about 20% of patients, including vertigo (12%), scalp necrosis or ulceration (8%), and a dry cough (6%).
European guidelines (2020) recommend that all patients with clinically suspected GCA have ESR, CRP and complete blood count with platelets.

The American College of Rheumatology guidelines (2021) recommend that patients with suspected GCA have a unilateral temporal artery biopsy wiith a > 1 cm specimen within 2 weeks of starting oral glucocorticoids. Biopsy is recommended over ultrasound or MRI of the carotid artery for establishing the diagnosis. Noninvasive vascular imaging is recommended to establish the extent of large vessel involvement.

Normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is helpful in ruling-out GCA or TA in the corticosteroid naive patient (LR− 0.2). However, the diagnosis may uncommonly occur in patients with an erythrocyte sedimentation <50 mm/hour.
However, an elevated ESR (>100) is only minimally helpful in ruling-in TA (LR+ 1.9).

A systematic review identified 68 studies with just over 14,000 patients with possible giant cell arteritis (GCA). They concluded that platelet count greater than 400,000/microliter and an ESR greater than 100 mm/h were best at ruling in GCA when it was suspected (LR+ 3), while ESR <40 mm/h was best at ruling out (LR- 0.18, 95% CI 0.08-0.44).

Duplex ultrasound imaging showing a "halo sign" has good sensitivity and specificity and is recommended for all patients per European guidelines. One study in 451 consecutive patients with giant cell arteritis found 92% sensitivity and 96% specificity (LR+ 22, LR− 0.09). A study of 40 newly diagnosed patients with giant cell arteritis compared the intima media thickness with 40 age and sex matched controls. They identified a cutoff of 0.42 mm as having 100% sensitivity and 97% specificity for the diagnosis of superficial temporal arteritis.

However, another study of Doppler USN found only 63% sensitivity, but 100% specificity, meaning that a positive USN was diagnostic for temporal arteritis. However, this study suffered from verification bias, since not all patients underwent the reference standard of biopsy.

Temporal artery biopsy of the affected side has traditionally been the gold standard in confirming TA, and should still be considered for all patients, especially if color duplex ultrasound is equivocal. Need at least 2 cm of tissue. If biopsy is negative but clinical suspicion is high, consider a biopsy of the contralateral side.
Patients being started on a course of corticosteroids should have a baseline eye and bone density examination.
MRI, 18F-FDG PET and PET/CT all have similar accuracy to color duplex ultrasound.
For patients with ESR that is elevated out of proportion to CRP, order serum protein electrophoresis and urine Bence-Jones protein to evaluate for multiple myeloma.
Order a baseline metabolic laboratory profile and screen for osteoporosis and infection if you plan to start corticosteroids.
Suspect giant cell arteritis in patients with new onset headache associated with visual symptoms or jaw claudication, especially if over age 50 years.
Apply ACR diagnostic criteria; normal ESR makes GCA less likely.
Corticosteroid treatment should be started if clinical suspicion is strong pending biopsy confirmation.

British guidelines (2020) suggest that for patients in whom GCA is likely (> 50%), an abnormal ultrasound may obviate the need for biopsy. Temporal artery biopsy with or without ultrasound is recommended for all other patients. The exception is patients where the likelihood is considered low (< 20%) who have a normal ultrasound.

Begin treatment with prednisone 40 to 60 mg/day immediately for patients in whom giant cell arteritis (GCA) is the most likely diagnosis. Do not wait for temporal artery biopsy before beginning treatment.A
Consider IV pulse therapy (methylprednisolone 250 mg q 6 hours) for 3 days for patients with visual loss or stroke.B
Consider treatment with methotrexate in addition to corticosteroids to reduce relapses and total amount of steroids used. B
Taper the dose of steroids slowly at 2.5 to 5.0 mg/day every 2 weeks until at 25 mg a day and then even more slowly after that. C

Relapses are common and are managed by starting steroid therapy again or increasing dose to previous level. Treatment is usually required for 2 to 3 years. The monoclonal antibody tocilizumab improved the likelihood of steroid free remission.C
First line therapy is prednisone, 40 to 60 mg/day. If clinical suspicion is high do not wait for temporal artery biopsy results before initiating treatment.

Continue this dose until symptoms resolve and ESR returns to normal (usually 2-6 weeks) then begin a slow taper. Reduce dose by 2.5 to 5.0 mg a day every 2 weeks until at 25 mg a day then more slowly after that. Typically will achieve dose of 7.5 to 10 mg per day after 6 months of therapy, followed by complete discontinuation after 1 to 2 years.
Consider high-dose IV pulse therapy (IV methlyprednisolone 250 mg IV every 6 hours for 3 days then oral prednisone 40-60 mg a day) if visual loss or stroke are present.

Relapses are common and are managed by starting steroid therapy again or increasing dose to previous level that controlled symptoms if still on steroids. Swedish guidelines recommend addition of tocilizumab for selected patients with relapsing disease for up to one year. Criteria for using tocilizumab include relapse during or after steroid treatment, biopsy verified arteritis, clinically active giant cell arteritis, elevated ESR or CRP, and patient is experiencing side effects of glucocorticoid treatment.

British guidelines (2020) recommend the following protocol for tapering corticosteroids. 1) Treat with 40 to 60 mg oral prednisolone until symptoms resolve and inflammatory biomarkers return to normal. At that point and while the daily dose is > 20 mg reduce the dose by 10 mg every 2 weeks. Between 10 and 20 mg dose of corticosteroids and while in clinical remission, reduce the dose by 2.5 mg every 2 to 4 weeks. When in clinical remission and the dose is <= 10 mg, reduce the dose by 1 mg every 1 to 2 months.

If the patient shows signs of clinical relapse characterized by headache alone, return to the previous higher prednisolone dose. If they have a relapse characterized by ischemic symptoms (jaw, tongue, or limb claudication), consider resuming high dose oral prednisolone at the original starting dose with or without a steroid sparing agent such as methotrexate. For patients with systemic symptoms or symptoms such as abdominal or back pain that may indicate involvement of the aorta, perform vascular imaging with CT or MRI and either increase oral prednisolone or add methotrexate.
Consider methotrexate therapy in addition to prednisone therapy. Use appears to decrease overall amount of prednisone needed and reduce relapses.

A trial randomized patients with giant cell arteritis (GCA) to the monoclonal antibody tocilizumab once or twice weekly during 26 or 52 week prednisone tapers. At one year, patients receiving the study drug had approximately half the total prednisone dose during the study period, with good safety. Sustained steroid free remission was significantly more likely in the treatment group (53% to 56% vs 14%, p <0.001, NNT = 2), and the drug was well tolerated.
The effectiveness of tocilizumab for patients with all three GCA phenotypes (cranial, extracranial and mixed) was confirmed in a prospective cohort study of 471 patients.

A case series described giving 18 patients with GCA 500 mg methylprednisolone IV daily for 3 days followed by tocilizumab monotherapy for one year. Most patients had relapse free survival up to 78 weeks after initiation of therapy.

A trial randomized of 54 patients with new onset or relapsing GCA to 300 mg secukinumab SC once weekly (an anti IL-17A monoclonal) or placebo. Sustained remission at 28 weeks was more likely in the intervention group (70% vs 20%). The drug was well tolerated.
A systematic review of 16 studies with 1068 participants confirmed the benefit of tocilizumab at reducing the likelihood of relapse (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.23-0.63).
Use of low-dose aspirin may reduce cranial ischemic complications.
Infliximab as maintenance therapy after steroid induced remission showed no benefit and possible harm.
Azathioprine treatment showed a significant lower corticosteroid requirement. Cholestatic jaundice in association with this drug has been observed.
A systematic review of Janus Kinase Inhibitors found only case series and 4 observational studies.
Anticipate 2 years or more of treatment.
Relapses may require an increase in dosage of medication or a reinstitution of steroids.
Patients suspected of TA should be referred for temporal artery biopsy.
Do not delay treatment with corticosteroids pending biopsy results.
If there is question about the diagnosis or if symptoms do not improve within 2 to 3 days of beginning treatment, consider consultation with rheumatology.
Patients with suspected visual impairment should be treated with corticosteroids immediately. When treatment is delayed for more than 1 day the prognosis for visual recovery is very poor.
Treat all patients on long-term corticosteroids with calcium and Vitamin D for prevention of osteoporosis and monitor for complications of steroid therapy.
Infections (OR 1.4) and hospitalization for infections (OR 2.7) are significantly more common in the year after diagnosis with GCA and corticosteroid treatment.
If untreated 20% to 30% of patients will experience unilateral or bilateral blindness.
Most patients will begin to see improvement within 24 to 72 hours of beginning therapy. C
Immediate treatment, within 24 hours, significantly reduces the risk of visual complications. A
TA is a self-limited disease lasting up to 2 years.
Long-term mortality is not affected, except perhaps in a subset of patients requiring hospitalization.
Left untreated 20% to 30% of patients will experience unilateral or bilateral blindness.
Immediate treatment, within 24 hours, significantly reduces the risk of visual complications; improvement typically begins within 24 to 72 hours. A
ESR and CRP return to normal within 2 to 4 weeks after beginning therapy.
Approximately 60% of patients will have a relapse of the disease.

The mortality rate of patients with TA is not significantly different than general population. However, there is evidence of increased frequency of life-threatening ischemic events such as myocardial infarction and cerebro-vascular accidents in the early course of the disease.
Monitor ESR every 4 weeks until resolution of symptoms.
Continue monitoring every 8 weeks for 12 to 18 months after stopping corticosteroids.
Temporal arteritis involves inflammation of large blood vessels. It is treated with steroids such as prednisone.
Symptoms usually improve within 24 to 72 hours after beginning treatment.
Treatment usually lasts about 2 years. If symptoms come back you should tell your doctor as you may need additional treatment.
Treatment should be started immediately to prevent blindness.
Disease occurs almost exclusively in patients older than 50 years of age.
